question: A patient develops violaceous flat-topped papules on the trunk three months after starting an ACE inhibitor. The lesions closely resemble lichen planus. What is the single most important next step?

answers.text: Perform a Grattage test to confirm psoriasis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The violaceous flat-topped morphology is not psoriasis (which gives erythematous plaques with silvery scale). The Grattage test supports a diagnosis of psoriasis, not lichen planus.

answers.text: Take a detailed drug history, because a lichenoid drug eruption can be clinically indistinguishable from idiopathic lichen planus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A lichenoid drug eruption can look identical to idiopathic lichen planus, so a detailed drug history is mandatory. Common culprits include ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, thiazides, antimalarials, and NSAIDs — the eruption typically resolves on withdrawal of the offending drug.

answers.text: Start systemic corticosteroids immediately without further investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While systemic steroids may eventually be used for severe lichen planus, the priority is to identify and withdraw a causative drug first. Treating a drug eruption without removing the trigger is ineffective.

answers.text: Order a KOH mount to exclude a fungal infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KOH mounts are used to identify fungal elements in suspected dermatophyte infections, not to evaluate violaceous papular lesions suggestive of lichen planus or a lichenoid drug eruption.

overallFeedback.feedback: When violaceous flat-topped papules appear after starting a new medication, always consider a lichenoid drug eruption. A detailed drug history is essential — ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, thiazides, antimalarials, and NSAIDs are common culprits, and withdrawal often resolves the eruption.
Correct. When LP-like lesions appear temporally related to a new drug, drug history is the decisive step — ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, thiazides, antimalarials, and NSAIDs are common culprits.
